fields.definition: A transition effect that emulates a vinyl record or turntable being abruptly braked to a standstill, produced by rapidly sweeping the playback speed, and therefore the pitch, of audio down to zero over a short time. It is typically applied to a full mix or a single element at the end of a phrase or before a drop.
fields.plain_english: It makes a sound slow down and drop in pitch, like a record player switched off while the record is still spinning. Producers use it to end a section with a dramatic wind-down.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a dramatic, instantly recognisable transition or ending gesture that signals the close of a phrase or section by mimicking a turntable losing power. This adds energy and a sense of release without changing the arrangement itself.
fields.practical_application: A technician automates a tape/vinyl-stop plugin or draws a downward pitch or varispeed automation curve on a track or the master bus, timed to hit on the last beat before a breakdown or drop.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with a true tape-stop, which follows a different slow-down curve than a spinning platter losing momentum
Making the effect too long so the wind-down drags and loses impact
Not lining the effect up to the beat grid, so the return into the next section feels loose
scenario_contexts: Ending an EDM section right before a drop or breakdown
Closing out the final bar of a track for a dramatic finish
Emulating a DJ-style turntable brake inside a DAW mix

sources: Sound on Sound (technique articles on transition/tape-stop effects)

fields.definition: A production technique in which a vocal recording is sliced into short fragments that are rearranged, re-pitched and re-triggered, often mapped across a sampler and played melodically, to create a rhythmic or melodic hook. The result is a new phrase built from pieces of the original performance.
fields.plain_english: It is when you cut a singing recording into tiny pieces. You rearrange the pieces like blocks to build a new catchy, rhythmic tune.
fields.purpose_function: It turns an existing vocal recording into a playable instrument or hook, letting a producer add a human-sounding melodic element without recording a new performance. This gives a track a distinctive, memorable motif.
fields.practical_application: A technician slices a vocal in a sampler or DAW, maps the slices across a keyboard or pad grid, then plays a fresh melodic or rhythmic pattern, often adding pitch and formant correction to keep it natural.
common_mistakes: Leaving clicks or pops at slice edit points instead of adding short fades or crossfades
Re-pitching slices far up or down without formant control, giving an unnatural chipmunk sound
Reusing a copyrighted vocal without clearing sample rights
scenario_contexts: Building a melodic hook for a future bass, pop or EDM track
Turning a full vocal take into a rhythmic stutter pattern
Creating a new topline for a remix from an acapella

sources: Sound on Sound (vocal editing and sampling technique articles)
